sources.citation: Eberhard, Simons & Fennig (eds.). 2019. Ethnologue, 22nd ed., entry 'Popoloca, Coyotepec' [pbf] (Internet Archive copy)
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Nothing on phonology. Dialects: San Vicente Coyotepec Popoloca, San Mateo Zoyamazalco Popoloca; 41% intelligibility of Otlaltepec [pow], 23% of Atzingo [poe], 15% of Tlacoyalco [pls]; 'San Mateo dialect may be a separate language'; Language Development: Dictionary; Writing: Unwritten.

sources.citation: DiCanio, Christian & Ryan Bennett. 2018 [2020]. Prosody in Mesoamerican languages (Oxford Handbook of Language Prosody), preprint
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: No mention of Coyotepec; Popolocan stress examples are Metzontla (Veerman-Leichsenring 1991), San Juan Atzingo (Kalstrom & Pike 1968) and Tlacoyalco (Stark & Machin 1977).

sources.citation: van der Hulst, Harry, Keren Rice & Leo Wetzels. 2010. The languages of Middle America. In van der Hulst, Goedemans & van Zanten (eds.), A survey of word accentual patterns in the languages of the world, 249-312. Berlin: De Gruyter Mouton. Sec. 5.1.5 Popolocan, pp. 267-268
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on Coyotepec. Reports second-hand: Metzontla Popoloca penultimate stress realised as duration (Veerman-Leichsenring 1984, 1991); Western Popoloca stressed syllable usually coincides with end of grammatical stem (Williams & Pike 1968: 379); Eastern Popoloca penultimate vowel of the stem stressed (Kalstrom & Pike 1968); Tlacoyalco consonant vs vowel stress (Stark & Machin 1977). None of these is the Coyotepec variety.

sources.citation: Veerman-Leichsenring, Annette. [2007]. Un documento popoloca del siglo XVIII: un estudio preliminar. Amerindia hors-serie. Paris: A.E.A.

sources.citation: Barrera, Bartolo & Karen Dakin. 1978. Vocabulario popoloca de San Vicente Coyotepec: popoloca-espanol, espanol-popoloca. Cuadernos de la Casa Chata 11. Mexico, D.F.: Centro de Investigaciones Superiores del INAH (CISINAH). 147 pp.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: print only (no digital copy found when the work was looked up)
sources.note: The only Coyotepec-specific description in existence; 1400-item vocabulary whose front matter (pp. 1-6) is the one place a Coyotepec stress/orthography statement could be; HLAS annotation and every later bibliography (Suarez 1983, Veerman-Leichsenring, Laver 1994, MacLaury 1986) cite it as the Coyotepec source. Out of print (CIESAS 1993: SOLD OUT), no digital copy located.

sources.citation: Williams, Ann F. & Eunice V. Pike. 1968. The phonology of Western Popoloca. Lingua 20: 368-380.
sources.tag: likely states stress; not yet obtained
sources.access_detail: online with a university library login
sources.note: Suarez 1983 groups Coyotepec with Western Popoloca and Ethnologue gives 41% intelligibility with Otlaltepec; the closest described variety with an explicit stress statement (stress usually at the end of the grammatical stem, p. 379, per van der Hulst et al. 2010). Would only ever be a related-variety proxy, not a Coyotepec statement.
